screens.title: Chaos Engineering Principles and Practice on AWS
screens.narratorSegment: Chaos engineering is a deliberate, scientific approach to uncovering weaknesses before they become outages. In this chapter we will learn why injecting controlled faults—when done safely—makes your systems more observable, resilient, and easier to operate under pressure. You will see how to define a measurable steady state, build a hypothesis, choose a minimal blast radius, and automate experiments so they become repeatable. We will also walk through AWS Fault Injection Simulator as a practical tool to inject faults like instance terminations or network latency and to wire stop conditions that protect production. Throughout, I will emphasize safety: design experiments with measurable success criteria, integrate CloudWatch alarms as automatic stop conditions, and use least-privilege IAM roles. A concrete example you will study is terminating one EC2 instance in an Auto Scaling Group and verifying that the group self-heals while customer-facing metrics remain within defined thresholds. By the end of this chapter you will be able to design a safe experiment, run it with FIS, interpret the results, and convert findings into actionable improvements. Consider: what critical metric would you choose as your steady state for your primary service?

Chaos Engineering Principles and Practice on AWS
Build confidence by testing failure modes with controlled experiments using AWS Fault Injection Simulator.
In this lesson

You will learn core principles, how to design safe experiments, run FIS templates, observe stop conditions, and analyze outcomes to increase resilience.

Proactive fault injection reveals hidden failure modes, improves alerts, and reduces downtime by turning surprises into planned improvements.

Well-planned, automated experiments increase confidence. Safety nets like stop conditions are mandatory for production tests.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Over the next screens you will build four practical skills tied to chaos engineering. First, you will explain the discipline and its measurable goals: what steady state means and why a hypothesis matters. For example, you should be able to define an SLI such as p99 latency under 100 milliseconds and describe why it is a steady-state indicator. Second, you will design experiments safely: pick a small blast radius, identify impact scenarios, and plan rollback steps. A concrete practice is to plan terminating a single instance in an Auto Scaling Group while having a CloudWatch alarm as a stop condition. Third, you will operate AWS Fault Injection Simulator to create experiment templates that target resources and actions; you will learn to attach stop conditions and use least-privilege IAM roles. Fourth, you will analyze experiment results: compare observed metrics against your hypothesis, document findings, and convert discoveries into prioritized remediation. Each of these objectives has a short verification milestone so you can practice them safely before increasing scope.

screens.title: What is Chaos Engineering?
screens.narratorSegment: Start with a precise definition: chaos engineering is the discipline of experimenting on a system in order to build confidence in its capability to withstand turbulent conditions in production. That means intentionally injecting faults, but doing so under control: with a hypothesis, measurable steady-state metrics, and safety guards. A concrete example is hypothesizing that terminating one EC2 instance in an Auto Scaling Group will not reduce application success rate below 99%. You design an experiment, choose a small blast radius, run the fault, observe behavior, and then conclude whether the system met the hypothesis. A common misconception is that chaos engineering is reckless or random disruption. It is not. It is scientific: you predict, test, observe, and learn. Another pitfall is assuming tests in staging are sufficient; real traffic patterns and cross-system dependencies often only appear in production-like conditions. Finally, the ethical and operational boundaries matter: always include stop conditions, communicate with teams, and automate rollback plans. To check your understanding: can you name a steady-state metric for a critical A P I you own and explain why it signals user impact?

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.10 › What is Chaos Engineering?
Chaos engineering — concise definition
Experiment on systems to build confidence they handle real-world turbulence.
Core idea
  • • Hypothesize steady state for measurable metrics.
  • • Inject faults that mimic real-world events.
  • • Observe, verify, rollback, and document findings.
Analogy
Like a fire drill for software: rehearse failures to uncover gaps before an actual outage.
Key Takeaway

Treat experiments as hypotheses to validate, not as chaos for its own sake.

Common Mistake

Running experiments without a steady-state definition or stop conditions risks uncontrolled impact.

Concrete example
Hypothesis: If a single EC2 instance in our ASG is terminated, Auto Scaling replaces it and the HTTP 200 success rate remains above 99%.
Explanation
  • • Define the steady state metric: HTTP 200 success rate, p99 latency.
  • • Choose blast radius: one instance, one AZ, or 1% of traffic.
  • • Select stop condition: CloudWatch alarm for error rate or healthy host count.
Reflection

Which SLI in your environment best reflects user impact? How small can your blast radius be and still provide useful signal?

screens.title: Core Principles of Chaos Engineering
screens.narratorSegment: There are five core principles that structure every effective chaos experiment. First, hypothesize about steady-state behavior: pick measurable indicators such as success rate, p99 latency, or healthy host count and state what 'normal' means. Second, vary real-world events: choose faults that mirror realistic failures like instance termination, network latency, or database unavailability so your test reveals practical weaknesses. Third, run experiments in production when appropriate: lower environments are useful for rehearsal, but production uncovers real traffic patterns and dependencies — only do this with strict controls. Fourth, automate experiments so they are repeatable and can be scheduled or run as part of pipelines; this removes human error and lets you gather consistent data over time. Fifth, minimize blast radius: affect the smallest subset of users or services initially and increase scope only after validating safety. A common misconception is that automation removes the need for planning — in fact, automation must be grounded in a solid hypothesis and safeguards like stop conditions. As you follow this process, you will iteratively harden your systems and your teams' response capabilities. Core Principles of Chaos Engineering means hypothesize steady state, vary realistic faults, test safely (production with caution), automate, and keep blast radius minimal.. In practical terms, a repeatable process: hypothesize, vary, run, automate, minimize blast radius. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 12 › Chapter 12.10 › Core Principles
The process
A repeatable sequence to keep experiments safe and informative.
1
Hypothesize steady-state
Choose measurable SLIs like p99 latency or success rate and state expected behavior.
2
Vary real-world events
Select faults that mimic realistic failures such as instance termination or network latency.
3
Run experiments safely
Start small; if in production use tight stop conditions and notify responders.
4
Automate for repeatability
Make experiments scripts or templates to collect consistent data and enable scheduling.
5
Minimize blast radius
A single instance or small percentage of traffic reduces risk while giving actionable signal.
Key Takeaway

Follow the process to keep experiments safe and their results trustworthy.

Practical checklist
  • • Define the steady-state metric and threshold.
  • • Pick the minimal blast radius and communication plan.
  • • Prepare monitoring and a CloudWatch alarm for stop conditions.
  • • Automate the experiment in FIS or a runbook and test in staging first.
Misconception
Automation without hypothesis is not better than manual chaos. Always tie automated runs to measurable predictions.
Pro Tip

Start with scheduled small experiments to build team confidence, then expand scope as you establish safe practices.

screens.title: Designing and Executing Safe Experiments
screens.narratorSegment: Designing a safe experiment is a sequence of deliberate steps. Begin by defining a steady state: pick measurable SLIs such as HTTP 200 success rate or healthy host count and record baseline values. Next, formulate a clear hypothesis—what you expect to occur when the fault is introduced. For example, you might hypothesize that terminating a single EC2 instance will not reduce the success rate below 99%. Identify potential impact and worst-case scenarios, then choose a minimal blast radius—one instance, one availability zone, or a tiny percentage of traffic. Prepare the inject action and the tools you will use, such as AWS FIS, and set automatic stop conditions using CloudWatch alarms that reflect critical user-facing metrics. Plan rollback actions you can execute immediately if alarms trigger. During execution, monitor your steady-state metrics; if the hypothesis holds, record the evidence and expand the scope gradually on future runs. Document all findings and convert surprising results into prioritized action items. A common mistake is skipping the pre-run checklist or missing a rollback plan—both invite uncontrolled incidents. Ask yourself: what single alarm would immediately indicate unacceptable user impact for this experiment?

screens.title: AWS Fault Injection Simulator (FIS) — Example Template
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Fault Injection Simulator enables managed, repeatable chaos experiments by letting you define targets, actions, and stop conditions in an experiment template. The template typically contains a description, targets that identify specific resources or selection modes, actions that perform the fault (for example, terminate an EC2 instance), stop conditions that reference CloudWatch alarms as automatic circuit breakers, and an IAM role for FIS to assume. A concrete example is a template that selects one instance from an Auto Scaling Group using COUNT(1) and a tag filter, then calls the terminate-instances action with that selection. The stop condition would reference an alarm like TargetGroupHealthyHostCount or an application error-rate alarm, so the experiment is stopped automatically if important metrics degrade. A misconception is that granting broad permissions to FIS is convenient; in practice you must apply least privilege and only allow the actions and resource ARNs required by the experiment. After a run, compare observed metrics to your hypothesis and convert findings into prioritized fixes. What CloudWatch alarm would you choose as the most conservative stop condition for your application? keyIdea.text: An FIS experiment template defines targets, actions, stop conditions and the IAM role used to run the experiment.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.10 › FIS Template Example
Example FIS Template (simplified)
This JSON defines targets, actions and a stop condition for a safe experiment.
{
  "description": "Terminate a random EC2 instance in a specific ASG",
  "targets": {
    "OneEc2InstanceInAsg": {
      "resourceType": "aws:ec2:instance",
      "selectionMode": "COUNT(1)",
      "resourceArns": [
        "arn:aws:ec2:us-east-1:123456789012:instance/i-0abcdef1234567890",
        "arn:aws:ec2:us-east-1:123456789012:instance/i-0abcdef1234567891"
      ],
      "filters": [
        {
          "path": "Tags.Name",
          "values": ["MyWebAppInstance"]
        }
      ]
    }
  },
  "actions": {
    "TerminateInstance": {
      "actionId": "aws:ec2:terminate-instances",
      "parameters": {
        "instanceIds": "${OneEc2InstanceInAsg}"
      }
    }
  },
  "stopConditions": [
    {
      "source": "aws:cloudwatch:alarm",
      "value": "arn:aws:cloudwatch:us-east-1:123456789012:alarm:MyCriticalAppAlarm"
    }
  ],
  "roleArn": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/FISExperimentRole"
}
Explanation
  • • targets: selects the specific EC2 instances by ARN or tag and a selection mode of COUNT(1).
  • • actions: the AWS API call to perform, here terminate-instances using the selected instance IDs.
  • • stopConditions: a CloudWatch alarm ARN that will automatically stop the experiment if triggered.
  • • roleArn: an IAM role granting FIS the minimum permissions needed for the actions.
Key Takeaway

Stop conditions give you an automatic circuit breaker. Tie them to user-facing alarms whenever possible.

Security Note

Grant FIS least privilege: only the actions and resource ARNs required by the experiment.

screens.title: Benefits, Common Mistakes, and Operational Outcomes
screens.narratorSegment: Chaos engineering delivers several clear operational benefits: it increases resilience by uncovering hidden failure modes, improves observability by forcing better metrics and alerts, enhances incident response through repeated practice, reduces downtime by addressing weaknesses proactively, and can also surface cost savings by revealing inefficient fault tolerance mechanisms. A concrete example: an experiment that exposes a slow database connection during peak traffic can prompt changes to connection pooling or retries, reducing future outages and wasted compute. Common mistakes include running experiments without a defined hypothesis, neglecting stop conditions, granting overly broad IAM permissions to FIS, or assuming staging test results fully predict production behavior. Another error is an overly large blast radius on a first run; this converts learning into outages. Operationally, results from experiments should be documented and turned into prioritized action items—patches, improved monitoring, runbook updates, or architecture changes. A useful question to close with is: after your next experiment, what one operational improvement will you prioritize based on the evidence? keyIdea.title: Benefits & pitfalls
keyIdea.text: Chaos engineering increases resilience and observability but requires hypotheses, stop conditions, least-privilege, and small initial blast radii to be safe.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.10 › Benefits & Mistakes
Benefits
  • • Increased resilience: find and fix failure modes before customers do.
  • • Improved observability: experiments highlight blind spots and missing alerts.
  • • Better incident response: practice reduces reaction time and confusion.
  • • Reduced downtime and potential cost savings from optimized fault tolerance.
Example Outcome

An experiment that exposed DB connection exhaustion led to connection pool tuning and an immediate reduction in errors under load.

Common Mistakes
  • • No hypothesis or steady-state: tests become noise and give no actionable insight.
  • • Missing stop conditions: experiments can escalate into real outages.
  • • Overly broad permissions for FIS: unnecessary risk from accidental actions.
  • • Large blast radius too early: lessons should come from small, controlled scope.
Action

After each experiment produce a short report: hypothesis, observations, whether it held, and 2–3 prioritized remediation tasks.

screens.title: Analyzing Experiment Results
screens.narratorSegment: After an experiment finishes, your work is only beginning. Analysis means comparing the hypothesis you wrote before the run with the actual system behavior you observed. Start by collecting the steady-state metrics you defined: success rate, p99 latency, healthy host counts, and error rates. Pull the same metrics from immediately before, during, and after the fault injection so you can see trends and transient spikes. A concrete example: if your hypothesis said an Auto Scaling Group will keep HTTP 200 success above 99% when an instance is terminated, check the application success rate and target group healthy hosts during the termination window. If success dips below the threshold but recovers quickly, note the time to recovery and whether customers saw errors. If it never recovers, the experiment revealed a critical weakness. Pay attention to root-cause signals: increased latency in downstream services, queue depth growth, or elevated C P U on replacement instances. A common misconception is to treat any error during the experiment as failure — instead, distinguish between expected transient degradation that meets acceptance criteria and uncontrolled failures that violate steady-state. Document exact timestamps, metric deltas, and logs that correspond to observed anomalies. Finally, convert each unexpected result into an action item: change alert thresholds, add retries, adjust capacity, or fix slow database queries. Ask yourself: did this experiment validate our resilience or reveal a systemic gap we must prioritize?

A common misconception is to treat any error during the experiment as failure — instead, distinguish between expected transient degradation that meets acceptance criteria and uncontrolled failures that violate steady-state. Document exact timestamps, metric deltas, and logs that correspond to observed anomalies. Finally, convert each unexpected result into an action item: change alert thresholds, add retries, adjust capacity, or fix slow database queries. Ask yourself: did this experiment validate our resilience or reveal a systemic gap we must prioritize?

keyIdea.title: Compare hypothesis to evidence
keyIdea.text: Use pre-defined steady-state metrics and logs to decide whether the system met expectations and what remediation is required.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.10 › Analyzing Experiment Results
Hypothesis
A clear, measurable prediction to test.
Example: "Terminate one instance; success rate stays ≥ 99% and p99 latency < 300ms." Record the exact metrics and threshold values for later comparison.
Observed Outcome
Measured behavior during the experiment window.
Capture time-series charts and raw logs. Note transient spikes and recovery times. Tag logs with experiment id for traceability.
Deviation & Root Cause
Where the system diverged and why.
Link anomalies to components: load balancer, ASG latency, DB queue growth, or insufficient IAM permissions affecting automation. Prioritize fixes by user impact.
Evidence Panel
Snapshots, charts, and notes you use to judge the experiment.
Core Metric
Metric Comparison
Steady-state
Success rate: 99.9%
p99 latency: 120ms
During experiment
Success rate: 98.5% (2 min dip)
p99 latency: 420ms (spike)
Interpretation: short-lived latency spike exceeded hypothesis threshold and caused a small, brief customer impact. Root cause traces show slow DB connection provisioning on replacement instance.
Concrete Example
Action item: pre-warm database connections during instance launch, tighten health check thresholds to avoid routing traffic to under-prepared instances, and add a CloudWatch alarm for p95 latency during scaling events.
Key Takeaway
Careful comparison of hypothesis and evidence turns a failed expectation into concrete improvements that raise real resilience.

screens.title: Interpreting FIS Stop Conditions and Alarms
screens.narratorSegment: A stop condition is your experiment's emergency brake. In AWS FIS, stop conditions are typically CloudWatch alarms that, when triggered, tell FIS to halt the running experiment automatically. The practical result is a circuit breaker: if a critical metric crosses a safety threshold, the experiment stops before it can escalate. That matters because many failures manifest as sudden metric spikes — increased HTTP 5xx, a drop in healthy target count, or rising error rates in downstream services. Choosing which alarms to link is a balance. Use alarms that reflect user-facing health: request success rate, healthy host count for the target group, or a critical application alarm you already rely on. Also add infrastructure alarms for C P U or disk saturation that would indicate a broader problem. A concrete example: link a CloudWatch alarm that monitors TargetGroupHealthyHostCount. If the count drops below your expected minimum, the alarm goes to ALARM and FIS stops the experiment. A common misconception is to use many noisy, low-value alarms; this creates false stops. Instead, pick a few high-signal alarms and set thresholds conservatively for an experiment blast radius. Document your stop condition strategy during experiment design, test it in a sandbox, and make sure your incident response runbook explains how stop conditions interact with rollbacks and notifications.

keyIdea.title: Stop conditions protect production
keyIdea.text: Link minimal, high-signal CloudWatch alarms to FIS experiments as automatic circuit breakers to prevent uncontrolled impact.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.10 › Stop Conditions & Alarms
Stop Conditions Explained
Automatic safety gates that halt experiments when key alarms fire.
Choose high-signal alarms
Select alarms tied to user impact such as healthy host counts, 5xx rate, or errors in critical pipelines. These directly reflect customer experience.
Set conservative thresholds
Too-tight thresholds will stop experiments prematurely. Use recent historical data to pick realistic cutoffs for your blast radius.
Test your stop conditions
Run dry-runs in staging to validate alarms will trigger as expected and integrate with notification channels so teams see stops immediately.
Example Alarm Definition
{ "AlarmName": "ASG-HealthyHosts-Low", "MetricName": "HealthyHostCount", "Namespace": "AWS/ApplicationELB", "Statistic": "Minimum", "Period": 60, "EvaluationPeriods": 1, "Threshold": 1, "ComparisonOperator": "LessThanThreshold" }
If this alarm enters ALARM during an experiment, FIS will see the stop condition and immediately halt the experiment, preventing further instance terminations or injected faults.
Common mistake

Attaching many noisy alarms that fire for unrelated reasons creates false stops. Prefer fewer, high-value alarms and validate them with historic data.

screens.title: IAM and Least-Privilege for FIS Experiments
screens.narratorSegment: Security matters when you run automated fault injection. Use an IAM role for FIS that grants only the actions required to run the experiment and nothing more. The chapter emphasizes least privilege: allow actions like ec2:TerminateInstances or rds:RebootDBInstance only for the specific resources your experiment targets, and include read permissions for CloudWatch alarms so FIS can watch stop conditions. A practical approach is to create a role named FISExperimentRole and scope its resource ARNs to the ASG or instance ARNs used in the experiment, rather than using wildcards that apply across the account. A concrete example is to permit ec2:DescribeInstances and ec2:TerminateInstances on the specified instance ARNs and to allow cloudwatch:DescribeAlarms for the alarm ARNs used as stop conditions. Also attach the AWS managed policy AWSFaultInjectionSimulatorServiceRole as a baseline if appropriate, then remove any excess actions you don't need. A common misconception is to assume FIS needs full EC2 or RDS access; it does not. Overly broad roles increase blast radius and make accidental damage easier. Finally, include an audit step: record the role's ARN and the experiment template, and restrict who can update experiment templates via IAM policies. This keeps control over what faults can be injected and who can authorize them.

keyIdea.title: Least-privilege FIS roles
keyIdea.text: Create FIS service roles with only the necessary actions on specific resource ARNs and ensure CloudWatch read access for stop conditions.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.10 › IAM for FIS
Role Design Pattern
Service role scoped to experiment resources with minimal actions.
Minimal Actions
  • ec2:DescribeInstances
  • ec2:TerminateInstances (scoped ARNs)
  • cloudwatch:DescribeAlarms
Scoping Resources
Prefer explicit resource ARNs for your ASG, instances, or RDS instances. Avoid giving blanket access to all resources in the account.
Sample policy fragment (illustrative)
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": [
    "ec2:DescribeInstances",
    "ec2:TerminateInstances",
    "cloudwatch:DescribeAlarms"
  ],
  "Resource": ["arn:aws:ec2:us-east-1:123456789012:instance/*"]
}
Scope the Resource value to the exact ARNs used by your experiment in production to minimize blast radius.
Operational Controls
Audit who can create or edit FIS templates. Restrict template creation to a small set of engineers and require reviews. Keep a change log linking template versions to experiment runs.
Risk note

If the IAM role is too broad, an attacker or misconfigured experiment could terminate large swaths of infrastructure. Least privilege reduces that risk.

Pro tip

Use separate roles for staging and production experiments. Validate role permissions in a safe sandbox before granting production access.

screens.title: Running a Basic FIS Experiment: Guided Steps
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough describes the safe, observable process of running a basic AWS FIS experiment to terminate a single EC2 instance in an Auto Scaling Group. First, prepare prerequisites: ensure an ASG with two or more instances exists, the instances carry a tag you can filter on, you have an IAM role for FIS with least privilege, and a CloudWatch alarm that will act as a stop condition is in place. Next, create an experiment template that selects COUNT(1) on instances with your tag and defines the action to terminate that instance. Save the template but do a dry run in a staging environment first. When you start the experiment in production with a very small blast radius, watch CloudWatch metrics and the experiment run details. Observe the EC2 console: one instance should transition to terminated and the ASG should launch a replacement. Monitor your steady-state metrics: did HTTP success rate, p99 latency, or healthy host counts stay within hypothesis bounds? If the stop condition alarm fires, FIS will stop automatically — confirm the experiment status changed to stopped and the environment stabilizes. Finally, collect timestamps, instance IDs, and metric windows for post-run analysis. A common mistake is to skip the dry run; always validate templates and alarms in a non-production environment first. After the run, debrief, document findings, and schedule remediation items.

keyIdea.title: Observe, verify, stop
keyIdea.text: Prepare prerequisites, validate templates in staging, run with small blast radius, and use alarms to halt the experiment if things go wrong.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.10 › Lab Walkthrough
Step-by-step
  1. Verify prerequisites: ASG with multiple instances, tagged instances, FIS IAM role, and a CloudWatch stop alarm.
  2. Create and save an experiment template. Use COUNT(1) selection to limit blast radius for the first run.
  3. Dry-run the template in staging. Confirm the alarm behavior and that the experiment stops when an alarm is triggered.
  4. Start a controlled experiment in production with monitoring engaged and stakeholders notified.
  5. Observe EC2 and ASG behavior, CloudWatch metrics, and FIS run status. Stop immediately if metrics breach your hypotheses.
Verify Observation

Confirm the ASG replaced the terminated instance and that the application remained within steady-state thresholds or note the exact deviation.

Terminal / Console Callouts
While the chapter focuses on the console workflow, these are the observation steps you would take in any interface: capture instance IDs, note the ASG activity history, and export the CloudWatch metric windows around the experiment time. Below is an example snippet you might record for documentation.
# Experiment record
ExperimentId: fis-experiment-12345
Start: 2024-01-15T10:32:00Z
TargetInstance: i-0abcdef1234567890
ASGAction: terminated -> new instance i-0abcdef9876543210 launched
CloudWatch: SuccessRate dip 99.9% -> 98.4% (10:32:10 - 10:34:00)
Checkpoints
  • Stop condition did not fire / or fired — note which.
  • Replacement instance passed health checks in X seconds.
  • Any customer-facing errors and their durations.

screens.title: Documenting, Remediating, and Iterating
screens.narratorSegment: A disciplined post-experiment workflow turns chaos into meaningful, lasting resilience gains. Immediately after an experiment, gather a concise package: your hypothesis, the experiment template used, the blast radius, stop conditions, metric windows, relevant logs, and timestamps for observed anomalies. This package should be attached to a post-experiment report that lists findings and recommended action items. For each unexpected behavior, create a remediation ticket with a clear owner, priority, and acceptance criteria tied to measurable metrics. For example, if an experiment shows p99 latency spikes during instance replacement, an action could be to add connection pooling or pre-warm caches and then define an acceptance test that reproduces the previous spike but keeps p99 below your steady-state threshold. Iterate: schedule a follow-up experiment after fixes to validate improvements. A common misconception is to treat a single experiment as conclusive; instead, run variations over time and after infrastructure changes to build cumulative confidence. Also update runbooks and on-call procedures with lessons learned so incident response improves. Finally, share sanitized findings with stakeholders so teams can prioritize architecture, code, or monitoring changes. The end goal is not to cause failure but to surface and systematically close gaps so customer impact becomes increasingly rare.

keyIdea.title: Close the loop
keyIdea.text: Document experiments, convert surprises into prioritized action items, and run follow-up tests to validate fixes.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.10 › Remediation & Iteration
Post-Experiment Report
A standard template for repeatable analysis and action.
Contents
  • Hypothesis and steady-state definition
  • Experiment template id and role used
  • Observed metrics, logs, and timeline
  • Findings, root causes, and remediation items
Action Item Example
Add DB connection pre-warming during instance startup. Owner: DB team. Acceptance: p99 latency stays below 300ms during replacement events in follow-up experiment.
Iteration Cycle
After fixes, run targeted experiments to validate each remediation. Use the same steady-state metrics and keep blast radius small until proven safe. Track change over time to show increased confidence for stakeholders.
Misconception

A single successful experiment does not guarantee future resilience. Regular, automated experiments and monitoring are required to maintain confidence.

Why it matters

Closing the loop ensures chaos engineering leads to improved observability, better incident response, and fewer customer-facing outages over time.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part A
screens.narratorSegment: Reviewing key concepts helps you keep practical definitions close at hand. Chaos engineering is the practice of experimenting on systems to build confidence that they will behave under turbulent conditions. Steady-state behavior is the measurable baseline you define before an experiment — these are the metrics you will compare against. Blast radius describes the scope of impact from an experiment; minimize it first and increase only when you have confidence. These concepts guide safe experiments. Keep them short and actionable: hypothesis-driven experiments, scoped blast radius, automated stop conditions, and least-privilege service roles. Use these terms as a checklist before every run: have a hypothesis, define steady-state metrics, restrict the blast radius, attach stop conditions, and confirm IAM roles are scoped. A quick habit of referring to this checklist reduces risk and accelerates learning from each experiment.

Experimenting on systems to build confidence in their resilience under turbulent conditions.

The measurable normal state of the system defined by metrics like success rates and latency.

Module 12 › Chapter 12.10 › Key Concepts
AWS Fault Injection Simulator
Managed service for creating experiments that target AWS resources with controlled actions and stop conditions.
Experiment Template
A declarative definition of targets, actions, stop conditions, and the IAM role used for an experiment.

fullNarratorScript:
Chaos engineering is a deliberate, scientific approach to uncovering weaknesses before they become outages. In this chapter we will learn why injecting controlled faults—when done safely—makes your systems more observable, resilient, and easier to operate under pressure. You will see how to define a measurable steady state, build a hypothesis, choose a minimal blast radius, and automate experiments so they become repeatable. We will also walk through AWS Fault Injection Simulator as a practical tool to inject faults like instance terminations or network latency and to wire stop conditions that protect production. Throughout, I will emphasize safety: design experiments with measurable success criteria, integrate CloudWatch alarms as automatic stop conditions, and use least-privilege IAM roles. A concrete example you will study is terminating one EC2 instance in an Auto Scaling Group and verifying that the group self-heals while customer-facing metrics remain within defined thresholds. By the end of this chapter you will be able to design a safe experiment, run it with FIS, interpret the results, and convert findings into actionable improvements. Consider: what critical metric would you choose as your steady state for your primary service?

Over the next screens you will build four practical skills tied to chaos engineering. First, you will explain the discipline and its measurable goals: what steady state means and why a hypothesis matters. For example, you should be able to define an SLI such as p99 latency under 100 milliseconds and describe why it is a steady-state indicator. Second, you will design experiments safely: pick a small blast radius, identify impact scenarios, and plan rollback steps. A concrete practice is to plan terminating a single instance in an Auto Scaling Group while having a CloudWatch alarm as a stop condition. Third, you will operate AWS Fault Injection Simulator to create experiment templates that target resources and actions; you will learn to attach stop conditions and use least-privilege IAM roles. Fourth, you will analyze experiment results: compare observed metrics against your hypothesis, document findings, and convert discoveries into prioritized remediation. Each of these objectives has a short verification milestone so you can practice them safely before increasing scope.

This second objectives screen focuses on applying the skills in measurable ways. For explanation, you should be able to state what defines steady-state for a service and why a hypothesis must be measurable. For designing experiments, your milestone is to produce an experiment plan that lists metrics, blast radius, rollback steps, and a stop condition. For operating AWS FIS, you will create an experiment template that targets tagged EC2 instances and schedules a single termination action, verifying that permissions use least privilege. For analysis, your milestone is to present a short run report that compares observed metrics to the hypothesis, lists root causes for deviations, and assigns remediation owners. Each objective ties back to a short verification task so you can practice and demonstrate competency safely before scaling experiments to larger blast radii.

Start with a precise definition: chaos engineering is the discipline of experimenting on a system in order to build confidence in its capability to withstand turbulent conditions in production. That means intentionally injecting faults, but doing so under control: with a hypothesis, measurable steady-state metrics, and safety guards. A concrete example is hypothesizing that terminating one EC2 instance in an Auto Scaling Group will not reduce application success rate below 99%. You design an experiment, choose a small blast radius, run the fault, observe behavior, and then conclude whether the system met the hypothesis. A common misconception is that chaos engineering is reckless or random disruption. It is not. It is scientific: you predict, test, observe, and learn. Another pitfall is assuming tests in staging are sufficient; real traffic patterns and cross-system dependencies often only appear in production-like conditions. Finally, the ethical and operational boundaries matter: always include stop conditions, communicate with teams, and automate rollback plans. To check your understanding: can you name a steady-state metric for a critical A P I you own and explain why it signals user impact?

There are five core principles that structure every effective chaos experiment. First, hypothesize about steady-state behavior: pick measurable indicators such as success rate, p99 latency, or healthy host count and state what 'normal' means. Second, vary real-world events: choose faults that mirror realistic failures like instance termination, network latency, or database unavailability so your test reveals practical weaknesses. Third, run experiments in production when appropriate: lower environments are useful for rehearsal, but production uncovers real traffic patterns and dependencies — only do this with strict controls. Fourth, automate experiments so they are repeatable and can be scheduled or run as part of pipelines; this removes human error and lets you gather consistent data over time. Fifth, minimize blast radius: affect the smallest subset of users or services initially and increase scope only after validating safety. A common misconception is that automation removes the need for planning — in fact, automation must be grounded in a solid hypothesis and safeguards like stop conditions. As you follow this process, you will iteratively harden your systems and your teams' response capabilities. Core Principles of Chaos Engineering means hypothesize steady state, vary realistic faults, test safely (production with caution), automate, and keep blast radius minimal.. In practical terms, a repeatable process: hypothesize, vary, run, automate, minimize blast radius. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Designing a safe experiment is a sequence of deliberate steps. Begin by defining a steady state: pick measurable SLIs such as HTTP 200 success rate or healthy host count and record baseline values. Next, formulate a clear hypothesis—what you expect to occur when the fault is introduced. For example, you might hypothesize that terminating a single EC2 instance will not reduce the success rate below 99%. Identify potential impact and worst-case scenarios, then choose a minimal blast radius—one instance, one availability zone, or a tiny percentage of traffic. Prepare the inject action and the tools you will use, such as AWS FIS, and set automatic stop conditions using CloudWatch alarms that reflect critical user-facing metrics. Plan rollback actions you can execute immediately if alarms trigger. During execution, monitor your steady-state metrics; if the hypothesis holds, record the evidence and expand the scope gradually on future runs. Document all findings and convert surprising results into prioritized action items. A common mistake is skipping the pre-run checklist or missing a rollback plan—both invite uncontrolled incidents. Ask yourself: what single alarm would immediately indicate unacceptable user impact for this experiment?

AWS Fault Injection Simulator enables managed, repeatable chaos experiments by letting you define targets, actions, and stop conditions in an experiment template. The template typically contains a description, targets that identify specific resources or selection modes, actions that perform the fault (for example, terminate an EC2 instance), stop conditions that reference CloudWatch alarms as automatic circuit breakers, and an IAM role for FIS to assume. A concrete example is a template that selects one instance from an Auto Scaling Group using COUNT(1) and a tag filter, then calls the terminate-instances action with that selection. The stop condition would reference an alarm like TargetGroupHealthyHostCount or an application error-rate alarm, so the experiment is stopped automatically if important metrics degrade. A misconception is that granting broad permissions to FIS is convenient; in practice you must apply least privilege and only allow the actions and resource ARNs required by the experiment. After a run, compare observed metrics to your hypothesis and convert findings into prioritized fixes. What CloudWatch alarm would you choose as the most conservative stop condition for your application? AWS Fault Injection Simulator (FIS) — Example Template means an fis experiment template defines targets, actions, stop conditions and the iam role used to run the experiment.. In practical terms, how an fis template targets resources, actions, and stop conditions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Chaos engineering delivers several clear operational benefits: it increases resilience by uncovering hidden failure modes, improves observability by forcing better metrics and alerts, enhances incident response through repeated practice, reduces downtime by addressing weaknesses proactively, and can also surface cost savings by revealing inefficient fault tolerance mechanisms. A concrete example: an experiment that exposes a slow database connection during peak traffic can prompt changes to connection pooling or retries, reducing future outages and wasted compute. Common mistakes include running experiments without a defined hypothesis, neglecting stop conditions, granting overly broad IAM permissions to FIS, or assuming staging test results fully predict production behavior. Another error is an overly large blast radius on a first run; this converts learning into outages. Operationally, results from experiments should be documented and turned into prioritized action items—patches, improved monitoring, runbook updates, or architecture changes. A useful question to close with is: after your next experiment, what one operational improvement will you prioritize based on the evidence? Benefits, Common Mistakes, and Operational Outcomes means chaos engineering increases resilience and observability but requires hypotheses, stop conditions, least-privilege, and small initial blast radii to be safe.. In practical terms, what you gain from chaos engineering and how to avoid pitfalls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

After an experiment finishes, your work is only beginning. Analysis means comparing the hypothesis you wrote before the run with the actual system behavior you observed. Start by collecting the steady-state metrics you defined: success rate, p99 latency, healthy host counts, and error rates. Pull the same metrics from immediately before, during, and after the fault injection so you can see trends and transient spikes. A concrete example: if your hypothesis said an Auto Scaling Group will keep HTTP 200 success above 99% when an instance is terminated, check the application success rate and target group healthy hosts during the termination window. If success dips below the threshold but recovers quickly, note the time to recovery and whether customers saw errors. If it never recovers, the experiment revealed a critical weakness. Pay attention to root-cause signals: increased latency in downstream services, queue depth growth, or elevated C P U on replacement instances. A common misconception is to treat any error during the experiment as failure — instead, distinguish between expected transient degradation that meets acceptance criteria and uncontrolled failures that violate steady-state. Document exact timestamps, metric deltas, and logs that correspond to observed anomalies. Finally, convert each unexpected result into an action item: change alert thresholds, add retries, adjust capacity, or fix slow database queries. Ask yourself: did this experiment validate our resilience or reveal a systemic gap we must prioritize?

A stop condition is your experiment's emergency brake. In AWS FIS, stop conditions are typically CloudWatch alarms that, when triggered, tell FIS to halt the running experiment automatically. The practical result is a circuit breaker: if a critical metric crosses a safety threshold, the experiment stops before it can escalate. That matters because many failures manifest as sudden metric spikes — increased HTTP 5xx, a drop in healthy target count, or rising error rates in downstream services. Choosing which alarms to link is a balance. Use alarms that reflect user-facing health: request success rate, healthy host count for the target group, or a critical application alarm you already rely on. Also add infrastructure alarms for C P U or disk saturation that would indicate a broader problem. A concrete example: link a CloudWatch alarm that monitors TargetGroupHealthyHostCount. If the count drops below your expected minimum, the alarm goes to ALARM and FIS stops the experiment. A common misconception is to use many noisy, low-value alarms; this creates false stops. Instead, pick a few high-signal alarms and set thresholds conservatively for an experiment blast radius. Document your stop condition strategy during experiment design, test it in a sandbox, and make sure your incident response runbook explains how stop conditions interact with rollbacks and notifications.

Security matters when you run automated fault injection. Use an IAM role for FIS that grants only the actions required to run the experiment and nothing more. The chapter emphasizes least privilege: allow actions like ec2:TerminateInstances or rds:RebootDBInstance only for the specific resources your experiment targets, and include read permissions for CloudWatch alarms so FIS can watch stop conditions. A practical approach is to create a role named FISExperimentRole and scope its resource ARNs to the ASG or instance ARNs used in the experiment, rather than using wildcards that apply across the account. A concrete example is to permit ec2:DescribeInstances and ec2:TerminateInstances on the specified instance ARNs and to allow cloudwatch:DescribeAlarms for the alarm ARNs used as stop conditions. Also attach the AWS managed policy AWSFaultInjectionSimulatorServiceRole as a baseline if appropriate, then remove any excess actions you don't need. A common misconception is to assume FIS needs full EC2 or RDS access; it does not. Overly broad roles increase blast radius and make accidental damage easier. Finally, include an audit step: record the role's ARN and the experiment template, and restrict who can update experiment templates via IAM policies. This keeps control over what faults can be injected and who can authorize them.

This walkthrough describes the safe, observable process of running a basic AWS FIS experiment to terminate a single EC2 instance in an Auto Scaling Group. First, prepare prerequisites: ensure an ASG with two or more instances exists, the instances carry a tag you can filter on, you have an IAM role for FIS with least privilege, and a CloudWatch alarm that will act as a stop condition is in place. Next, create an experiment template that selects COUNT(1) on instances with your tag and defines the action to terminate that instance. Save the template but do a dry run in a staging environment first. When you start the experiment in production with a very small blast radius, watch CloudWatch metrics and the experiment run details. Observe the EC2 console: one instance should transition to terminated and the ASG should launch a replacement. Monitor your steady-state metrics: did HTTP success rate, p99 latency, or healthy host counts stay within hypothesis bounds? If the stop condition alarm fires, FIS will stop automatically — confirm the experiment status changed to stopped and the environment stabilizes. Finally, collect timestamps, instance IDs, and metric windows for post-run analysis. A common mistake is to skip the dry run; always validate templates and alarms in a non-production environment first. After the run, debrief, document findings, and schedule remediation items.

A disciplined post-experiment workflow turns chaos into meaningful, lasting resilience gains. Immediately after an experiment, gather a concise package: your hypothesis, the experiment template used, the blast radius, stop conditions, metric windows, relevant logs, and timestamps for observed anomalies. This package should be attached to a post-experiment report that lists findings and recommended action items. For each unexpected behavior, create a remediation ticket with a clear owner, priority, and acceptance criteria tied to measurable metrics. For example, if an experiment shows p99 latency spikes during instance replacement, an action could be to add connection pooling or pre-warm caches and then define an acceptance test that reproduces the previous spike but keeps p99 below your steady-state threshold. Iterate: schedule a follow-up experiment after fixes to validate improvements. A common misconception is to treat a single experiment as conclusive; instead, run variations over time and after infrastructure changes to build cumulative confidence. Also update runbooks and on-call procedures with lessons learned so incident response improves. Finally, share sanitized findings with stakeholders so teams can prioritize architecture, code, or monitoring changes. The end goal is not to cause failure but to surface and systematically close gaps so customer impact becomes increasingly rare.

Reviewing key concepts helps you keep practical definitions close at hand. Chaos engineering is the practice of experimenting on systems to build confidence that they will behave under turbulent conditions. Steady-state behavior is the measurable baseline you define before an experiment — these are the metrics you will compare against. Blast radius describes the scope of impact from an experiment; minimize it first and increase only when you have confidence. These concepts guide safe experiments. Keep them short and actionable: hypothesis-driven experiments, scoped blast radius, automated stop conditions, and least-privilege service roles. Use these terms as a checklist before every run: have a hypothesis, define steady-state metrics, restrict the blast radius, attach stop conditions, and confirm IAM roles are scoped. A quick habit of referring to this checklist reduces risk and accelerates learning from each experiment.

These additional concepts focus on the artifacts and controls you must manage. AWS Fault Injection Simulator is the managed service for running chaos experiments on AWS; its experiment templates define targets, actions, and stop conditions. An experiment template is a reproducible artifact you version, review, and restrict to trusted roles. Stop conditions are CloudWatch alarms that automatically stop an experiment if critical thresholds are crossed; they are essential safety nets. Finally, hypothesis-driven design ensures each experiment tests a specific, measurable claim about system behavior so that outcomes map directly to actionable improvements. Keep templates small, auditable, and tied to concrete steady-state metrics so that every experiment is repeatable and reviewable.
